content: The cashew tree, scientifically known as Anacardium occidentale, belongs to the family Anacardiaceae. It is native to northeastern Brazil, where it is referred to as Caju for the fruit and Cajueiro for the tree in Portuguese. Today, the cashew tree is cultivated extensively in tropical climates for its cashew nuts and cashew apples. This small evergreen tree typically grows to a height of 10–12 meters and features a short, often irregularly shaped trunk. Its leaves are spirally arranged, leathery in texture, and range from elliptic to obovate in shape, measuring 4–22 cm in length and 2–15 cm in width, with smooth margins. The flowers of the cashew tree are produced in panicles or corymbs up to 26 cm long. Each flower is small, initially pale green, and later turns reddish. The flowers have five slender, acute petals that are 7–15 mm long. What appears to be the fruit of the cashew tree is actually an accessory or false fruit, known as the cashew apple, which develops from the receptacle of the cashew flower. The cashew apple is oval or pear-shaped and ripens into a yellow and/or red structure measuring approximately 5–11 cm in length. The true fruit of the cashew tree is a kidney-shaped or boxing-glove-shaped drupe that grows at the end of the cashew apple. The drupe develops first, followed by the expansion of the peduncle into the pseudo-fruit. Inside the true fruit is a single seed, commonly referred to as the cashew nut. While the cashew nut is considered a nut in culinary terms, it is botanically classified as a seed. The seed is encased in a double shell that contains a caustic phenolic resin called urushiol, a potent skin irritant also found in poison ivy. This resin can cause severe skin irritation, and some individuals are allergic to cashews, though they are a less common allergen compared to other nuts. The cashew tree is known by various vernacular names worldwide, including cajueiro, acajou, marañón, and pajuil, among others. In Puerto Rico and other parts of the Antilles, the pseudo-fruit is primarily consumed as raw fruit. The cashew industry originated in Brazil and was spread globally by the Portuguese. Cashew trees are now cultivated in regions with warm and humid climates, with production occurring in approximately 32 countries. As of 2005, the major producers of raw cashews were Vietnam (960,800 tons), Nigeria (594,000 tons), India (460,000 tons), Brazil (147,629 tons), and Indonesia (122,000 tons). The total global area under cashew cultivation is around 35,100 square kilometers. India has the largest area dedicated to cashew production, though its yields are relatively low. The global average yield is approximately 700 pounds per acre (780 kg per hectare). Vietnam, India, and Brazil collectively account for over 90% of all cashew kernel exports. Notably, Kollam (Quilon) in Kerala, India, produces around 4,000 tons of cashews annually and serves as a major trading center alongside Palasa, Mangalore, and Kochi. The cashew apple is valued for its juicy but acidic pulp, which can be consumed raw or used to make jams, chutneys, and various beverages. In some regions, its juice is processed and distilled into liquor or consumed as a refreshing drink called Cajuína. In Goa, India, the cashew apple is used to produce fenny, a locally popular distilled liquor. In Nicaragua, the cashew apple is consumed raw, made into juice, or processed into sweets, jellies, wine, and homemade vinegar. However, the cashew apple is highly perishable and contains significant amounts of tannin, leading to its frequent disposal after the cashew nut is removed. The urushiol in the dark green shells of cashew nuts must be removed before the seeds are processed for consumption. This is achieved through shelling, a hazardous process that often causes painful skin rashes similar to poison ivy among workers. In India, urushiol has been traditionally used by mahouts (elephant keepers) to control tamed elephants. Cashews labeled as raw in health food stores have been cooked but not roasted or browned. Cashew nuts are a common ingredient in Asian cuisine and can be ground into cashew butter, similar to peanut butter. Due to their high oil content, cashews are also used in other nut butters to enhance oil levels. Cashews contain 180 calories per ounce (6 calories per gram), with 70% of these calories derived from fat. The liquid within the shell casing of the cashew, known as Cashew Nut Shell Liquid (CNSL), has various industrial applications that were first developed in the 1930s. CNSL is fractionated through a process similar to petroleum distillation, yielding two primary products: solids used as friction particles in brake linings and an amber-colored liquid that is aminated to create phenalkamine curing agents and resin modifiers. Phenalkamines are primarily used in epoxy coatings for marine and flooring markets due to their intense hydrophobic properties and ability to remain chemically active at low temperatures.
